narrative:
Albert Einstein (1879–1955) announced himself to the world in what became known as his *annus mirabilis*: in 1905 he published four hugely influential papers in Switzerland [[9]], among them "On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies," which came to be known as his Special Theory of Relativity [[8]], and a paper on Brownian motion that provided the first incontrovertible evidence of atoms' existence [[13]]. That same year he explained the photoelectric effect — the phenomenon by which light striking a metal knocks out an electron, creating a small electrical current — using Max Planck's quantum theory [[4]]. Following Planck, Einstein claimed that light energy could occur in discrete packets, or quanta, later called photons, that could dislodge electrons from a metal surface [[4]], and he introduced the concept of "duality," the idea that light energy has a dual nature — somehow existing in two possible forms simultaneously [[4]].

Special relativity itself grew out of a pointed calculation: using Maxwell's theory, Einstein worked out the speed of a light beam as measured from a moving object such as a train [[1]]. The theory carried a consequence whose implications would prove enormous — the famous equation E=mc², establishing that mass and energy are equivalent [[7]][[8]]. This equivalence is not merely abstract: the mass that is shed when protons and neutrons combine is released as energy according to E=mc² [[1]], and it is precisely this mechanism that explains why the Sun shines [[2]].

A decade later, in 1915, Einstein offered an astonishing further explanation [[3]]: his General Theory of Relativity, in which he replaced Newton's picture of gravitational forces acting on apples and moons with an entirely new model based on geometry — the curvature of space and time [[2]][[5]][[12]]. His revised law of gravitation corrected Newton's by accounting for the delays at which gravity propagates [[6]], and it carried a striking further implication: anything that has energy possesses mass in the gravitational sense and is attracted accordingly [[6]]. A solar eclipse later confirmed the theory by showing that light travels on geodesics through curved space-time, the warping produced by the Sun's gravity [[12]]. Einstein also demonstrated that we cannot send signals faster than the speed of light, which showed that Newton's original gravitational law had to be wrong [[6]], and he noted a deep symmetry in his own equations: if you rotate space into time and time into space, the equations remain unchanged [[1]].

Einstein recognized a troubling loophole in general relativity: his equations initially predicted a universe that would collapse under its own gravity, so he attempted to solve the problem by adding a new term — the cosmological constant — which could act as a repulsive force to resist that collapse [[2]]. In 1935, together with his student Nathan Rosen, he introduced what is today called the Einstein-Rosen bridge, a theoretical passage through curved space-time [[3]]. Philosophically, he remained committed to what he called Objective Reality Theory — the conviction that the universe exists in a unique, definite state independent of any human observation — a position he advanced against the Copenhagen Interpretation of quantum mechanics, which he considered nonsense [[5]].

Einstein's work cast a long shadow beyond pure physics. In 1939, scientists led by Leo Szilard approached Einstein for his involvement in a series of letters warning the Belgian government not to sell uranium from their Congo mines [[9]], and Einstein joined Niels Bohr in writing directly to President Roosevelt to warn of the potential for nuclear weapons [[7]]; nuclear fission had by then been determined to release 200 MeV per uranium atom in direct accordance with E=mc² [[8]]. Yet his deepest aspiration remained a unified field theory — a single framework that would incorporate all of general relativity, encompass the Standard Model of subatomic particles, and yield finite results [[1]]. That goal remains unfinished: combining the Standard Model with Einstein's theory of gravity causes calculations to blow up and become infinite, rendering the hybrid theory useless [[3]], and so Einstein's grandest ambition endures as the defining open question at the frontier of modern physics.
